newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Failed Japan insurer sparks Asia solvency scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Failed Japan insurer sparks Asia solvency scrutiny.

text.p: The 200 billion yen failure of Nissan Mutual Life, the first in Japan for 50 years, has sparked a surge of calls about insurer solvency in the region, one of the sector's main ratings agencies told Reuters on Thursday.

"We've had a dramatic rise in inquiries from policyholders and brokers wanting to know whether firms they deal with around the region are stable and financially secure," a spokesman with Standard & Poor's in Tokyo told Reuters.

Growing pressure for life insurers to get claims paying ability ratings -- an assessment of assets against liabilities -- was also seen by Deborah Keating, executive officer with the Investment Savings and Insurance Association in New Zealand.
"I think it's likely to become an issue," she told Reuters.
"There is a move afoot to say that life insurance companies should have a claims paying rating, although that hasn't developed into anything at this stage," she added.

The collapse of Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co -- ordered by Japan's Finance Ministry to close on April 25 after the revelation that Nissan's liabilities exceeded assets by 200 billion yen (US$1.58 billion) -- was seen to have been brought about by circumstances unique to Japan.
Company president Hiroshi Yonemoto said the failure stemmed from the bursting of Japan's "bubble era" of inflated real estate and stock prices in the late 1980s.
Nissan Life offered products with high guaranteed returns paid for from stock yields which hit the company's bottom line when the market weakened.
"This continues to be a source of great problems for several life insurers in Japan," Paul Sinnott, consulting actuary with Tillinghast-Towers Perrin in Hong Kong, told Reuters.
But Sinnott said despite recent weak performances on other Asian stock markets, similar failures elsewhere were unlikely.
"In other areas the potential for failure is more to do with regulatory authorities and the rules they lay down for solvency requirements," Sinnott said.
In the wake of Nissan's failure, industry officials around the region have been at pains to say that life players in their markets would not meet the same fate.

A brush with a similar fate at Australia's National Mutual Ltd in the early 1990s, where reserves were depleted after a guaranteed return product was hit by a meltdown in property and equities, was seen as the perfect lesson.
"Life insurers in Australia now have far, far more conservative portfolio investments and very small exposure to property," said Tony Jackson, insurance analyst at Macquarie Equities.

Philippines Insurance Commissioner, Eduardo Malinis, told Reuters his country's investment regulations and insurance code was "very conservative" and he did not believe the Nissan experience would happen there.

In Thailand, rules requiring a minimum level of reserves, imposed after the collapse of two firms 30 years ago, were seen to still be working. However, a need for ratings after 12 new life licences were granted in March in addition to the 13 existing ones, was seen by one executive.

"In future we may require rating in order to show an ability of the management and quality of companies," said Chaiyot Tyachate, director and senior executive vice president of Muang Thai Life Assurance Co Ltd.

"The conditions in Japan resulting in Nissan Mutual's problem do not exist in Singapore," Law Song Keng, president of Singapore's Life Insurance Association (LIA), told Reuters in a written reply to questions.

But an LIA statment on April 4 warned: "Life insurance companies may have to revise their future bonus rates in view of the lower investment returns and outlook for the future". Some players, including market giant Great Eastern Life, said that bonus rates were being revised downwards.
With volatility a constant in many markets, combined with rapid expansion and fierce competition in the region's insurance industry, prudence was vital, said Thailand's Chaiyot.
"Insurance companies should adopt a conservative and prudent (approach to) administration, investment and new products because they have to be sure they can deliver future promises," Chaiyot said.
